vignette:
He is seventy-nine now, a South Asian man with a stooped back and thick, careful hands that still move as if they are lifting boxes even when they are empty. He lives alone in a small apartment and still works part-time in a warehouse, insisting that work keeps him “straight in the head.” Over several conversations, he tells his story slowly, circling around the worst parts before he can come close to them.

He is a young man when he goes to war. At the time, he believes endurance is simple: do what you are told, keep moving, do not think too much. He remembers heat, mud, metal, the smell of oil and blood mixing in the air. What stays with him most is not one battle but a series of moments that seem frozen outside of time—waiting for incoming fire, hearing someone nearby scream for his mother, seeing the body of a friend he had been joking with only hours before. He still remembers the strange silence that followed explosions, the brief dead space in which his ears rang and he could not tell if he was alive. He says that during combat he learned to make himself hard and narrow, to focus only on the next second. Back then, that helped him survive.

When the war ends, his body returns home long before the rest of him does. His family expects gratitude, discipline, normal life. He tries to give them that. He marries, finds work, keeps his hair trimmed, rises early, says little. For years he believes that if he does not speak about what happened, the memories will fade. Instead they become more deeply carved into him. He starts waking abruptly in the night, fists clenched, heart racing, certain for a few disoriented seconds that he is back under attack. His wife tells him he shouts in his sleep. Sometimes he pushes her away without meaning to. He begins sleeping lightly, never fully resting, and grows irritable over small things he later regrets.

He learns to avoid whatever stirs the memories. Firecrackers send a current through his whole body. News footage of war makes him leave the room. He does not attend veterans’ gatherings because he cannot bear the smell of uniforms and cigarettes together. Crowded places make him scan for exits without realizing he is doing it. Even at family celebrations, his shoulders stay tense, his eyes drawn to windows and doorways. He tells himself he is simply cautious, but inside he feels perpetually braced, as though danger has only stepped out briefly and may return at any time.

Work in the warehouse suits him because it offers order, routine, and physical labor. He likes shelves labeled correctly, boxes stacked square, the predictability of shipments arriving and leaving. The noise of machinery can still startle him, especially when something drops unexpectedly, and then for a moment he is no longer an old man at work but a young soldier with his pulse hammering in his throat. He covers these moments by turning away, pretending to check inventory until the wave passes. Coworkers know him as reliable, quiet, and strict about safety. They do not see how much effort it takes for him to stand with his back to an open loading bay, or how often he checks locks before closing up.

His marriage does not survive the years of distance he cannot explain. He says his wife grew tired of living with “half a man.” He does not say this bitterly, only with a flat sadness that suggests he has told himself this many times. After the divorce, his world becomes smaller. He keeps in contact with a few relatives but avoids telling them much. When his children were younger, he wanted to protect them from his temper and from the stories, so he stayed silent; now the silence feels permanent. Loneliness sits heavily on him, but closeness feels dangerous too. When someone asks direct questions about the war, he either goes blank or changes the subject.

In the present, he looks exhausted even when he has slept. He says his mind is never quiet. During the day, memories arrive uninvited—images of faces, sounds, fragments of terrible scenes that break into ordinary moments. He can be taping up a box or drinking tea and suddenly feel the old terror as if it is happening again. He feels ashamed of how frightened he still gets, ashamed that after so many decades he cannot command his own nerves. He also carries guilt that has outlived the war: guilt that he survived when others did not, guilt over things he did and failed to do, guilt that seems impossible to set down.

What stands out most is how long he has been living this way. He has built a life around control, work, and silence, but the war remains present inside him, not as history but as something unfinished. Even now, nearing eighty, he moves through the world as though part of him is still waiting for the next explosion.
